newsitem.title: FRANCE: Paris underground train bomb kills two, wounds 48.
newsitem.headline: Paris underground train bomb kills two, wounds 48.

text.p: Two people were killed and 48 injured when a gas-canister bomb blew out the side of a regional express train in a Paris underground station during the early evening rush hour on Tuesday, officials said.

No one claimed responsibility, but the target, the timing and the type of bomb bore all the hallmarks of attacks in the capital last year by Moslem fundamentalists fighting against Algeria's French-backed military rulers.
President Jacques Chirac called the attack "a barbaric and terrorist act" and vowed that France would do everything in its power to fight terrorism.
Seven of the wounded were in critical condition, three of them fighting for their lives, and 28 were seriously injured, rescue officials said.
The explosion occurred in the fourth carriage of the RER train at 6.05 p.m. (1705 GMT) as it drew into the Port Royal station on the Left Bank.
"We heard a big explosion. They told us 'get out, get out' but we couldn't breathe because there was so much smoke. It was panic, fear," said one passenger who was on the train.

The bomb was placed inside a 15-kg (33 lb) gas canister which had been packed with nails, similar to those used by the Algerian fundamentalists last year, when eight people were killed and more than 160 injured, justice sources said.

"We see no difference from last year's attacks," a fire service captain said. Investigators found fragments of the gas canister on the spot. The body of one of the victims had been mutilated by nails.
Yves Bonnet, a former head of France's DST counter-espionage service, said: "Only the Algerian Islamic Armed Group (GIA) threatens France with this kind of attack."
Anti-terrorism investigating magistrates Jean-Louis Bruguiere, Laurence Le Vert and Jean-Francois Ricard were charged with probing the explosion.

The blast at the junction of Boulevard Montparnasse and Boulevard Saint-Michel occurred just two stops away from the Saint-Michel station, where eight people were killed and 86 wounded in an attack blamed on Algerian extremists in July 1995.
"We have no indication on the origin. It is an explosive device placed in a train carriage," Prime Minister Alain Juppe told reporters at the scene of the blast.
He ordered Interior Minister Jean-Louis Debre to put a security plan codenamed Vigipirate back into force immediately.

The plan, applied across France during last year's wave of attacks from July to October, involved intensive patrols by police, paramilitary gendarmes and soldiers at public transport stations, at public buildings and in the streets.
Border controls, virtually eliminated under a European Union open-border agreement, were reinstituted on Tuesday night.
Debre's chief of staff Michel Besse said after a meeting of police chiefs that several hundred CRS anti-riot police would be deployed at potential targets from Wednesday.
Besse said troops would also patrol Paris train stations, airports and public transport, and other cities.
Chirac said: "I would like to state...my determination, that of the government and of the whole nation to fight with all means against all forms of terrorism."
About half of the wounded were on the platform when the device went off.

"I thought immediately about last year's bombings," said 20-year-old student Remy Jiemza. "There were women crying, people panicked, some people fell to the ground, others were bleeding. Everyone was suffocating."

An American resident in Paris who was walking past said: "I saw people pouring out of the train with blood all over their faces and jackets. The first policeman was there within a minute and the first ambulances arrived within 10 minutes."

France is also facing a bombing campaign by Corsican separatist guerrillas, who blew up Juppe's Bordeaux mayoral office in October. But the outlawed Corsican National Liberation Front (FLNC) usually takes great care to avoid casualties.

Dozens of suspected Moslem fundamentalists were detained in round-ups across the country while police tracked down one small group believed responsible for a botched attack against a high-speed TGV train near Lyons.
Police killed the group's presumed leader Khaled Kelkal in a shoot-out following a long manhunt.
